{{Short description|Term in combinatorial game theory}}
{{About|the concept from combinatorial game theory|the board game Star|Star (board game)|the board game *Star|*Star|other game topics|Star (disambiguation)}}
In [[combinatorial game theory]], '''star''', written as '''{{math|&lowast;}}''' or '''{{math|&lowast;1}}''', is the value given to the game where both players have only the option of moving to the [[zero game]]. Star may also be denoted as the [[surreal form]] '''{{math|{{mset|0{{!}}0}}}}'''. This game is an unconditional first-player win.

Star, as defined by [[John Horton Conway|John Conway]] in ''[[Winning Ways for your Mathematical Plays]]'', is a value, but not a [[number]] in the traditional sense. Star is not zero, but neither [[positive number|positive]] nor [[negative number|negative]], and is therefore said to be [[fuzzy game|''fuzzy'']] and ''confused with'' (a fourth alternative that means neither "less than", "equal to", nor "greater than") 0. It is less than all positive [[rational number]]s, and greater than all negative rationals.

Games other than {0 | 0} may have value &lowast;. For example, the game <math>*2 + *3</math>, where the values are [[nimbers]], has value &lowast; despite each player having more options than simply moving to 0.

==Why &lowast; ≠ 0==
A [[combinatorial game]] has a positive and negative player; which player moves first is left ambiguous. The combinatorial game&nbsp;[[zero (game)|0]], or '''{&nbsp;|&nbsp;}''', leaves no options and is a second-player win. Likewise, a combinatorial game is won (assuming optimal play) by the second player [[if and only if]] its value is&nbsp;0. Therefore, a game of value&nbsp;&lowast;, which is a first-player win, is neither positive nor negative. However, &lowast; is not the only possible value for a first-player win game (see [[nimber]]s).

Star does have the property that the [[sum of combinatorial games|sum]] {{nowrap|&lowast; + &lowast;}}, has value 0, because the first-player's only move is to the game&nbsp;&lowast;, which the second-player will win.

==Example of a value-&lowast; game==
[[Nim]], with one pile and one piece, has value &lowast;. The first player will remove the piece, and the second player will lose. A single-pile Nim game with one pile of ''n'' pieces (also a first-player win) is defined to have value &lowast;''n''. The numbers &lowast;''z'' for [[integer]]s ''z'' form an infinite [[field (mathematics)|field]] of [[Characteristic (algebra)|characteristic]] 2, when addition is defined in the context of combinatorial games and multiplication is given a more complex definition.
